title: Large-Scale Networks

html:
Beyond individual modules, fMRI and tractography reveal functionally cohesive networks that link distant regions to perform complex cognitive functions. The default-mode network (DMN; medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate/precuneus, hippocampus) is engaged during rest, introspection, and episodic simulation - supporting internal scene construction and memory recall. The frontoparietal control (executive) network (dorsolateral PFC, lateral parietal) sustains task rules and goals during cognitive effort, integrating sensory input with working memory. The salience network (anterior insula, dorsal ACC) detects behaviorally relevant cues and acts as a switch: it suppresses DMN and engages executive regions when novel or salient events occur. In practice, these networks reflect core architectural motifs: the DMN overlaps hubs for multi-modal memory and affect, the executive network overlaps regions receiving BG-thalamic feedback, and the salience network overlaps areas receiving subcortical arousal/reward input. Together they coordinate global information flow - e.g. shifting between exploration (DMN-driven model updating) and exploitation (executive-driven action) - essential for adaptive world modeling. Whole-brain models connect species-specific structural wiring to neural activity (Figure) 1. Competitive interactions improve model fit across human, macaque, and mouse brains (Figure).

Dense within-module connectivity (clustering coefficient  0.5-0.7) and sparse between-module connections ( 0.1-0.2)

Many tasks involve competition between networks. A classic example is the competition between FPN and DMN in attention tasks: stronger FPN activity suppresses DMN, enabling focus. However, there are also cooperative interactions: e.g. the hippocampus (DMN) and FPN co-activate when retrieving memory-guided rules. Neuromodulators provide a coarse level of coordination: e.g. dopamine and noradrenaline shifts can globally increase gain in FPN/SN or in sensory areas depending on motivational state

However, interactions are not solely competitive. Cooperative dynamics also occur, where different networks co-activate and synchronize their activity to support complex cognitive functions. For example, tasks that require retrieving memory-guided rules or engaging in creative thought can involve co-activation of the FPN and DMN. The Salience Network is believed to play a pivotal role in orchestrating these inter-network dynamics, particularly in switching the brain’s dominant processing mode between internal focus (DMN engagement) and external task-orientation (FPN/CEN engagement) based on the perceived relevance of internal or external stimuli. This "triple network model" (SN, DMN, CEN) highlights how the brain flexibly allocates its processing resources.

Dynamic Network Switching

These networks are not static anatomical entities but are better understood as dynamic coalitions of brain regions. The specific regions participating in a network and the strength of their interactions can vary depending on the ongoing cognitive state, task demands, and even individual differences. Despite this variability, a set of core, consistently identified networks forms the backbone of the brain’s functional organization.

This leads us to a broader principle: thia dynamic reconfiguration of functional circuits is a highly efficient mechanism for allocating limited neural resources. Instead of maintaining all possible processing pathways in an active state simultaneously-which would be metabolically exorbitant and could lead to widespread interference-the brain flexibly "wires up" the necessary circuits on demand. This allows a finite anatomical structure to support an impressively vast repertoire of cognitive functions and adaptive behaviors.

Brain alternates between segregated states (modules operating independently) and integrated states (increased between-module communication) based on task demands

State transitions occur on 100-500ms timescales, orchestrated by subcortical neuromodulators

Flexibility of network reconfiguration correlates with cognitive performance (r = 0.4-0.6)
